question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Ecologist Ines Maddock's hypothesis predicts that, per square meter of gravel bed, restored river reaches shelter more caddisfly larvae than channelized reaches.
• A survey team sampled one restored reach and one channelized reach of the Wendle River.
• Samplers searched for the same number of hours in each reach and counted every larva they found.
• In the restored reach, the samplers counted 270 larvae across 90 square meters of gravel bed.
• In the channelized reach, the samplers counted 180 larvae across 30 square meters of gravel bed.
• Both reaches were sampled in the same week of August.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the survey indicates about Maddock's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The survey supports Maddock's hypothesis, since the restored reach yielded 270 larvae, a larger count than the 180 larvae found in the channelized reach.
answer_b: The survey runs counter to Maddock's hypothesis, since the channelized reach held more larvae per square meter of gravel bed than the restored reach did.
answer_c: The survey cannot bear on Maddock's hypothesis, since only one restored reach and one channelized reach of the Wendle River were sampled.
answer_d: The survey only partly bears out Maddock's hypothesis, since the restored reach yielded more larvae overall even though it also covered more gravel bed.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. Maddock's hypothesis concerns larvae per square meter of gravel bed, so the raw totals cannot settle it; the counts have to be compared with the area searched. The restored reach had 270 larvae across 90 square meters, or 3 larvae per square meter. The channelized reach had 180 larvae across 30 square meters, or 6 larvae per square meter. Because the channelized reach held twice as many larvae per square meter, the survey's results are the opposite of what the hypothesis predicts, so they run counter to it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It is true that the restored reach yielded 270 larvae and the channelized reach 180, but the hypothesis is about larvae per square meter of gravel bed, not total counts. The restored reach was three times as large (90 versus 30 square meters), so its larger total does not show a higher density, and the density actually favors the channelized reach.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The notes do say that one restored reach and one channelized reach were sampled, but the samplers searched for equal hours and counted every larva in the areas given, which produces a density figure for each reach. Those figures can be compared directly with the hypothesis's prediction, so the survey does bear on it. A single pair of reaches is a limited sample, but it still supplies a density for each kind of reach to compare with the prediction, so it does not make the survey irrelevant to the hypothesis.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The restored reach did yield more larvae overall and did cover more gravel bed, but the hypothesis predicts a difference in larvae per square meter, and that is the measure that decides it. On that measure (3 versus 6 per square meter) the result goes against the hypothesis rather than partly agreeing with it.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Art historian Perrin Halloway has claimed that every surviving woodblock print made by the Odeline workshop carries the workshop's red seal in the lower right corner.
• A recent survey examined all 23 surviving woodblock prints made by the Odeline workshop.
• Twenty-two of the prints carry the red seal in the lower right corner.
• The remaining print, held at the Amberlaine Museum, carries no seal anywhere on the sheet.
• The workshop's own account book lists the Amberlaine print among the work it delivered to a patron.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the evidence in the notes indicates about Halloway's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The survey supports Halloway's claim, since 22 of the 23 surviving prints made by the Odeline workshop carry the red seal in the lower right corner.
answer_b: The survey neither supports nor undermines Halloway's claim, since it records where the red seal appears on 22 surviving prints rather than whether every print carries one.
answer_c: The evidence shows that Halloway's claim cannot be true as stated, since one surviving print that the workshop's account book lists among its work carries no seal, although the other 22 carry it.
answer_d: The evidence shows that Halloway was wrong to treat the red seal as a regular mark of the workshop, since one surviving print listed in the workshop's account book carries no seal.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. Halloway's claim is universal: it says that every surviving print from the workshop carries the red seal. The notes show that 22 of the 23 prints do, but the Amberlaine print has no seal anywhere, and the workshop's own account book lists it among the work the workshop delivered, so it is shown to be workshop work. A claim about every print cannot be true if even one documented print lacks the seal, so the survey contradicts the claim as stated. Choice C is also the only choice whose stance accounts for both the 22 sealed prints and the one documented exception, without treating either as decisive on its own.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It is true that 22 of the 23 prints carry the seal, but Halloway claimed that every print does. The Amberlaine print, which the account book shows to be workshop work, has no seal, so the survey cannot be said to support a claim about every print.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The survey does bear on the claim. Halloway said that every surviving print carries the seal, and the survey examined all 23 surviving prints and found one without it. The survey therefore tests exactly what the claim asserts, so the position of the seal on the other 22 prints does not make the findings irrelevant.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The unsealed print does show that Halloway's claim is false as stated, but 22 of the 23 surviving prints carry the seal, so the notes do not support the conclusion that the seal was not a regular mark of the workshop. One exception among 23 prints does not show that the workshop's practice was irregular.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• For decades, geologists attributed the circular pits of the Orlen Plain to the rainwater account: cool rainwater seeping downward dissolved buried limestone until the roof above it collapsed.
• In 2024, the Tessel survey team proposed the brine account: warm, salty brine rising from deep rock dissolved the limestone, and the roof above it then collapsed.
• Both accounts predict that a pit will occur only where limestone lies beneath it.
• The rainwater account predicts that water standing in the pits will be cool and nearly fresh, like local rainfall and rivers.
• The brine account predicts that water standing in the pits will be warm and salty.
• The team mapped 38 pits and found limestone beneath every one.
• The water in all 38 pits was warm and several times saltier than the nearby rivers.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the Tessel survey's findings indicate about the two accounts. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Because the water in all 38 pits was warm and salty, as the brine account predicts, the survey favors the brine account over the rainwater account.
answer_b: Because limestone lay beneath all 38 pits, as the rainwater account predicts, the survey supports the rainwater account over the brine account.
answer_c: Because limestone lay beneath all 38 pits, as both accounts predict, the survey cannot tell the rainwater account from the brine account.
answer_d: Because limestone lay beneath all 38 pits and the water in them was warm and salty, the survey shows both accounts to be partly correct.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it takes the stance that the full set of notes warrants. The notes say both accounts predict limestone beneath the pits, so that finding cannot separate them. The accounts differ in what they predict about the water: the rainwater account predicts cool, nearly fresh water, and the brine account predicts warm, salty water. The survey found that the water in all 38 pits was warm and several times saltier than the nearby rivers, which matches the brine account's prediction and contradicts the rainwater account's. The survey therefore favors the brine account over the rainwater account.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The limestone finding is true, but the notes say both accounts predict limestone beneath the pits, so it gives the rainwater account no special support. The one prediction on which the accounts differ, the condition of the water, was not met by the rainwater account, because the water was warm and salty rather than cool and nearly fresh.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It is true that both accounts predict limestone beneath the pits, so that finding alone cannot tell them apart. But the notes also give a prediction on which the accounts differ, the condition of the water, and the survey's result matched only the brine account. Ignoring that result leads to the mistaken conclusion that the survey cannot distinguish the accounts.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It accurately reports that limestone lay beneath all 38 pits and that the water in them was warm and salty. However, limestone beneath the pits was predicted by both accounts, so it does not distinguish them or show either one to be partly correct. The warm, salty water contradicts the rainwater account's central prediction that the water would be cool and nearly fresh, so the survey does not show that account to be even partly correct.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Historian Halden Pryce argued that Tessmouth's potteries did not assign each worker a single task until the Wenlow Canal opened in 1741; before the canal, he argued, every Tessmouth pottery relied on single-craftsman production.
• Newly examined ledgers show that three Tessmouth potteries were already assigning each worker a single task in 1733.
• The Wenlow Canal opened in 1741.
• After the canal opened, the larger orders that cheap barge delivery of clay made possible led more potteries to adopt single-task assignment, and eleven used it by 1755.
• The owners of two of the three potteries that used the system in 1733 signed a 1739 petition asking for the canal to be built.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the dated records indicate about Pryce's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The rise from three potteries to eleven by 1755, after the canal's larger orders led more potteries to adopt the system, supports Pryce's claim that the canal brought the system to Tessmouth.
answer_b: Since three potteries were already assigning each worker a single task in 1733, the records show that the canal had no bearing on the system, contrary to Pryce's claim that it did not appear until the canal opened.
answer_c: Since the owners of two of those three potteries signed a 1739 petition for the canal, the records show that the system led to the canal, reversing Pryce's claim that the canal brought the system to Tessmouth.
answer_d: Since three potteries were already assigning each worker a single task in 1733, eight years before the canal opened, the records undermine Pryce's claim that the system did not appear until the canal opened.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. Pryce claims that no Tessmouth pottery assigned each worker a single task until the canal opened in 1741. The notes show that three potteries were already using that system in 1733, eight years before the canal opened. That directly contradicts the claim that the system did not appear until the canal opened, so the dated records undermine Pryce's claim. The later spread to eleven potteries does not change this, because it concerns how widely the system caught on after 1741, not whether it existed before then.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The rise from three potteries to eleven by 1755 is accurate, and the notes say the canal's larger orders helped the system spread. But Pryce's claim is that the system did not appear until the canal opened, and three potteries were already using it in 1733. Faster spread after 1741 does not show that the canal brought the system to Tessmouth.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The 1733 dates do show that the canal did not introduce the system, but the notes also say that the larger orders made possible by the canal led more potteries to adopt the system. The canal therefore played a part in how the shift developed, so "no bearing" goes further than the records allow.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It is true that owners of two of the early potteries signed the 1739 petition for the canal, but the notes give no reason for their signing and say nothing about the system leading anyone to seek the canal. Claiming that the records show the system led to the canal reverses the causal direction without any support in the notes.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2019, sports scientist Ilka Odanel proposed that counting aloud lowers a basketball player's free-throw accuracy.
• Odanel reasoned that counting aloud competes with the step-by-step attention that novice shooters, whose shooting is not yet automatic, give to each shot.
• Odanel stated that her hypothesis concerns novice shooters only and makes no prediction about experienced shooters.
• In 2026, the Thornquist Sport Lab tested 48 experienced shooters, each with at least ten years of league play.
• Each shooter took 30 free throws while counting aloud and 30 free throws in silence.
• Accuracy was 78% in both conditions.
• Some commentators have cited the Thornquist result as evidence against Odanel's hypothesis.

The student wants to accurately characterize how the Thornquist Sport Lab's result bears on Odanel's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The Thornquist result undermines Odanel's hypothesis, since counting aloud did not lower free-throw accuracy among 48 shooters with at least ten years of league play.
answer_b: The Thornquist result neither supports nor undermines Odanel's hypothesis, since the 48 shooters, each with at least ten years of league play, belong to a group it makes no prediction about.
answer_c: The Thornquist result supports Odanel's hypothesis, since 48 shooters with at least ten years of league play were no less accurate when counting aloud, as shooters whose shooting is automatic would be expected to be.
answer_d: The Thornquist result narrows Odanel's hypothesis, since counting aloud did not lower accuracy among 48 shooters with at least ten years of league play, showing that its effect is limited to novices.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The notes state that Odanel's hypothesis concerns novice shooters only and makes no prediction about experienced shooters, and that the Thornquist Sport Lab tested 48 shooters, each with at least ten years of league play. Because every shooter in the study falls outside the group the hypothesis addresses, an accuracy of 78% in both conditions neither supports nor undermines it. Choice B is the only one that takes a stance consistent with both the stated limit of the hypothesis and the group the lab studied.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It is true that counting aloud did not lower accuracy among the 48 experienced shooters, which is why some commentators have cited the result against the hypothesis. But Odanel's hypothesis makes no prediction about experienced shooters, so a result from that group cannot count against it. Her claim about novices was not tested.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The experienced shooters did hold their accuracy while counting aloud, and Odanel did reason that novices' shooting is not yet automatic. But the hypothesis predicts nothing about experienced shooters, so their unchanged accuracy cannot count as agreement with it. Only a test with novice shooters could support it.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Odanel herself stated that her hypothesis concerns novice shooters only, so the study did not narrow it. The lab also tested no novices, so its result cannot show that the effect exists for novices, let alone that it is limited to them.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Agronomist Tobias Renquist hypothesized that field pea yield rises steadily as more crushed-shell lime is spread on acidic soil.
• Researchers at Brackenfold Station tested four lime rates on matched plots: 0, 2, 4, and 8 tonnes per hectare.
• Plots given no lime yielded 2.0 tonnes of peas per hectare.
• Plots given 2 tonnes of lime yielded 2.6 tonnes per hectare.
• Plots given 4 tonnes yielded 2.4 tonnes per hectare, and plots given 8 tonnes yielded 2.1 tonnes per hectare.
• Each lime rate was applied to six plots in the same season.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the trial's results indicate about Renquist's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Because the plots at every rate of lime applied out-yielded the plots with no lime, the trial confirms Renquist's hypothesis that pea yield rises steadily with the amount of lime applied, although the size of the gain differed from rate to rate.
answer_b: Although the 2-tonne plots out-yielded the plots with no lime, the 8-tonne plots yielded only 0.1 tonne more than the unlimed plots, so the trial shows that lime has no real effect on pea yield, contrary to Renquist's hypothesis.
answer_c: Although the plots at every rate of lime applied out-yielded the plots with no lime, yields were highest at 2 tonnes and lower at 4 and 8, so the trial supports a benefit from lime but not the steady rise Renquist's hypothesis predicts.
answer_d: Because yield fell as the lime rate rose from 2 to 8 tonnes, the trial reverses Renquist's hypothesis, showing that spreading lime lowers the pea yield of acidic soil.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. Renquist's hypothesis makes a specific prediction: yield should keep rising as the lime rate rises. The notes show a gain at every rate (2.6, 2.4, and 2.1 tonnes per hectare, all above the 2.0 of the unlimed plots), so lime does appear to help. But the gain was largest at the lowest rate, 2 tonnes, and shrank at 4 and 8 tonnes, so the steady rise the hypothesis predicts did not appear. Choice C is the only one that credits the benefit while rejecting the predicted pattern.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It is true that every lime rate beat the unlimed plots, but the hypothesis predicts a steady rise with more lime, and yields fell from 2.6 to 2.4 to 2.1 tonnes as the rate went up. A higher yield than the control does not confirm a prediction about how yield changes with the rate.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The 8-tonne plots did yield only slightly more than the unlimed plots (2.1 versus 2.0), but the 2-tonne and 4-tonne plots yielded 0.6 and 0.4 tonnes more. Lime did raise yield at every rate tested, so concluding that it has no real effect misreads the results.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Yield did fall as the rate rose from 2 to 8 tonnes, but it first rose from 2.0 to 2.6 tonnes per hectare between 0 and 2 tonnes of lime and stayed above the unlimed yield at every rate. Lime therefore raised yield at every rate tested; the pattern is a rise followed by a decline, not a reversal of the hypothesis showing that lime lowers yield.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Kestow Museum has long attributed a salt-glazed stoneware jug to the potter Edric Tamsen.
• Tamsen worked from 1740 to 1775 and dug his clay at the Wick Hollow pit.
• Corin Brandle, another potter, worked from 1760 to 1790 and also dug his clay at the Wick Hollow pit.
• Irene Colvane, a third potter, worked from 1790 to 1820 and dug her clay at Ferris Moor.
• A recent analysis found that the jug's clay matches clay from the Wick Hollow pit.
• The same analysis dated the jug's last firing to between 1762 and 1771.

The student wants to accurately characterize how the analysis bears on the museum's attribution of the jug to Tamsen. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The analysis is consistent with the museum's attribution to Tamsen but does not establish it, since the jug's clay and firing dates also fit Brandle, who dug from the same pit and worked in those years.
answer_b: The analysis confirms the museum's attribution to Tamsen, since the jug's Wick Hollow clay and its firing between 1762 and 1771 both fit the clay source and working years of Tamsen.
answer_c: The analysis counts against the museum's attribution to Tamsen, since the Wick Hollow clay of the jug was also dug by Brandle, who was working during the years in which the jug was fired.
answer_d: The analysis shows that Brandle rather than Tamsen made the jug, since Brandle used clay from the Wick Hollow pit and was working during the years in which the jug was fired.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. The notes say the museum attributes the jug to Tamsen, who worked from 1740 to 1775 and dug clay at Wick Hollow. The analysis found Wick Hollow clay and a last firing between 1762 and 1771, so the jug fits Tamsen. It also fits Brandle, who worked from 1760 to 1790 and used the same pit. Colvane is ruled out because she used Ferris Moor clay and worked from 1790, after the firing. The analysis therefore narrows the field, among the potters in the notes, to Tamsen and Brandle and is consistent with the attribution, but it cannot establish that Tamsen rather than Brandle made the jug.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The jug's clay and firing dates do fit Tamsen, but they fit Brandle equally well. Evidence that is consistent with the attribution does not confirm it when another potter also matches, so the analysis cannot establish that Tamsen made the jug.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It is true that Brandle also dug Wick Hollow clay and worked during the firing years, but this does not count against Tamsen. Tamsen matches the same evidence, and the analysis ruled out Colvane, so the attribution is no less supported than before.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Brandle does fit the clay source and the firing dates, but so does Tamsen, who also used the Wick Hollow pit and worked until 1775. Nothing in the notes allows the analysis to choose Brandle over Tamsen, so the analysis does not show that Brandle made the jug.
